Three of the appeals have been filed by the claimants for enhancement of the compensation awarded

view of the total amount awarded being acceptable to him. He may not have then been concerned

payload.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao
payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

payload.holding: The Court held that where passengers carried in a goods vehicle or tractor are gratuitous passengers whose risk is neither covered by statute nor by the insurance policy, the Claims Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct the insurance company to first pay the compensation and then recover it from the owner.
payload.ratio: In cases where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the terms of the insurance policy (such as gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle), the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act are not attracted, and neither the Claims Tribunal nor the High Court has the power to direct the insurer to pay the compensation and recover it from the owner.

args.question: Which judgments support reducing an award on appeal (quantum appeal by insurer), and which cut against me?

supporting.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
supporting.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent on the deceased is not entitled to compensation under 'loss of dependency'; only dependent legal representatives can claim under that head.
supporting.fact_alignment: Insurer appealed quantum on the ground that one claimant was gainfully employed and not dependent. The court agreed and reduced compensation by recalculating dependency and deduction.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent: the insurer's appeal on quantum succeeded, and the court actually reduced the award. It establishes that the insurer can successfully challenge the dependency calculation where a claimant is not genuinely dependent.
supporting.quote: a legal representative of a victim of a motor accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: The court can reduce the rate of interest on compensation on the insurer's appeal, even while upholding the principal quantum.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer appealed quantum; the court dismissed the appeal on quantum but reduced interest from 9% to 7.5% per annum.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that even where the principal quantum is upheld, the insurer can obtain meaningful relief by reducing the interest rate. Also establishes the important limitation that an insurer without Section 170 permission cannot challenge quantum.
supporting.quote: the interest should be reduced to 7.5% per annum

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: The court has power under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC to adjust compensation, including reducing interest rates, even when the insurer appeals.
supporting.fact_alignment: Insurer appealed quantum; court enhanced principal compensation but reduced interest from 7.5% to 6% per annum.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supports the proposition that interest rates can be reduced on appeal. Also confirms the court's wide power to modify awards under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC, which can work both ways.
supporting.quote: the prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum

supporting.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
supporting.principle: Contributory negligence (driving without licence and without helmet) justifies a 50% deduction from compensation.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Tribunal deducted 50% for contributory negligence where the injured rider had no licence and no helmet.
supporting.why_it_matters: If the facts of your case involve any contributory negligence by the victim (e.g., no helmet, no licence, driving on wrong side), this precedent supports a reduction in quantum on appeal.
supporting.quote: 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: Future prospects should not be added where the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer challenged addition of 50% towards future prospects for a deceased who was a fruit supplier (self-employed). The court held no addition for future prospects was warranted.
supporting.why_it_matters: Directly supports reducing quantum where the Tribunal wrongly added future prospects for a self-employed or temporary worker. This is a common error in Tribunal awards.
supporting.quote: Since the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment, he would not be entitled to any addition towards future prospects.

supporting.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
supporting.principle: The burden of proving contributory negligence lies on the party asserting it (the insurer). Where the insurer is already impleaded as a party, it can contest quantum on all grounds.
supporting.fact_alignment: Insurer appealed quantum and contributory negligence finding; court dismissed appeal but confirmed insurer's right to contest on all grounds when impleaded.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supports the insurer's right to challenge quantum on appeal when impleaded as a party (even without Section 170 permission). The ratio on burden of proof for contributory negligence is useful for framing arguments.
supporting.quote: Once the insurer is impleaded... it would be entitled to contest the claim petition by raising all grounds without being restricted to the statutory defences under Section 149(2)

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: The court can recalculate compensation on the insurer's appeal where the Tribunal applied wrong principles (e.g., wrong multiplier, wrong deduction, wrong future prospects).
supporting.fact_alignment: Insurer appealed quantum arguing income was assessed too high and future prospects wrongly applied. The court recalculated compensation using correct multiplier and deduction percentages.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that the insurer can successfully argue for recalculation where the Tribunal applied wrong multipliers or made computational errors. The court modified awards in multiple connected cases.
supporting.quote: the quantum of compensation awarded... stands modified

adverse.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
adverse.principle: An insurer without permission under Section 170 of the Motor Vehicles Act cannot challenge the quantum of compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will argue that your insurer client lacks standing to challenge quantum because it did not obtain Section 170 permission from the Tribunal. This is a jurisdictional bar that could get the appeal dismissed in limine.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This limitation applies only where the insurer was not impleaded as a party and the insured (owner) contested the claim. If the insurer was already impleaded as a party respondent (as in doc_018), or if the insured/owner failed to contest (collusion/absence), the insurer can challenge quantum on all grounds. Also, the insurer can always challenge on statutory defences under Section 149(2) and can argue computational/legal errors (wrong multiplier, wrong future prospects) as going to 'just compensation' rather than quantum per se.
adverse.quote: the Assurance Company cannot challenge the quantum of compensation without having permission under Section 170 of the Act

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC, the appellate court can enhance compensation even when only the insurer has appealed, because the court must award 'just compensation'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will argue that if the insurer appeals quantum, the court may use Order 41 Rule 33 CPC to enhance the award rather than reduce it. This is a real risk: the court in this very case enhanced compensation from ~Rs. 3.5 lakh to Rs. 5.99 lakh despite the insurer's appeal.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The enhancement risk is highest where the Tribunal's award is demonstrably below the Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi standards. If your Tribunal award already applies correct multipliers, future prospects, and deductions, the risk of enhancement is low. Also, the court reduced the interest rate in this case, showing it can adjust both ways.
adverse.quote: the court is duty-bound to award just compensation and may enhance the compensation amount under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC even in the absence of an appeal or cross-objections by the claimant

adverse.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
adverse.principle: The appellate court has a duty under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance inadequate compensation to ensure a 'just award', even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this for the proposition that an insurer's appeal opens the door to enhancement. The court here explicitly held that 'these proceedings being not truly adversarial' and that the court cannot 'close its eyes' to an inadequate award.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved clear errors in multiplier selection and failure to apply future prospects. If your Tribunal's award is already compliant with Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi standards, the risk of enhancement is minimal. The court's power under Order XLI Rule 33 is corrective, not punitive.
adverse.quote: the enhancement proposed is really in the nature of correction of the award on the basis of correct multiplier or principle or formula being applied in accordance with law laid down by the Supreme Court

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Where there is consistent oral testimony of an eye-witness, the Tribunal cannot impose contributory negligence based solely on a police sketch/site plan.
adverse.risk_to_client: If your appeal argues contributory negligence to reduce quantum, the opposing side will cite this to argue that the Tribunal's finding of no contributory negligence should not be disturbed unless the insurer led positive evidence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the specific fact that the insurer led NO evidence to rebut the eye-witness. If your case has independent evidence (e.g., site plan showing head-on collision, criminal court findings, or admissions in cross-examination), this precedent is distinguishable.
adverse.quote: once there is clinching oral evidence... that deceased was not negligent... the Tribunal cannot hold the deceased responsible for 50% negligence only on the basis of sketch/site plan

adverse.title: Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria vs Dilipkumar Ranchhodbhai Damor
adverse.principle: In injury cases, functional disability must be assessed in relation to the victim's vocation, and future prospects must be added even for self-employed persons.
adverse.risk_to_client: If your appeal challenges the disability assessment or future prospects in an injury case, the opposing side will cite this to argue that the Tribunal's assessment was correct or even inadequate.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This was a claimant's appeal for enhancement, not an insurer's appeal for reduction. The case involved amputation (severe disability). If your case involves minor injuries or a different factual matrix, this is distinguishable.
adverse.quote: the Tribunal fell for error in ignoring the functional disability in reference to the loss of future prospective income

adverse.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1 Has Filed The Written Statement To ...
adverse.principle: For a deceased below 40 years in stable employment, 50% must be added towards future prospects.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the Tribunal in your case correctly applied future prospects, the opposing side will cite this to argue the award was already correct. If the Tribunal under-applied future prospects, the court may enhance.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a Tribunal-level judgment, not binding on the High Court. The principle is already settled by Pranay Sethi. If your appeal challenges excessive future prospects (e.g., for a self-employed deceased), this case does not apply.
adverse.quote: 50% of actual income must be added towards future prospects

adverse.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
adverse.principle: The burden of proving contributory negligence lies on the insurer, and the Tribunal's finding on negligence is a finding of fact not lightly disturbed in appeal.
adverse.risk_to_client: If your appeal challenges a finding of no contributory negligence, the opposing side will argue that the insurer failed to discharge its burden of proof and that the finding of fact should not be disturbed.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The insurer in this case led NO evidence. If your case has evidence (site plan, criminal judgment, admissions), this is distinguishable. Also, the court confirmed the insurer's right to contest on all grounds when impleaded, which helps your side.
adverse.quote: the burden of proving contributory negligence lies on the party asserting it

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the insurer proves a policy breach (invalid licence), the court may order pay-and-recover but the quantum of compensation itself is not reduced.
adverse.risk_to_client: If your appeal is about quantum only (not liability), the opposing side will argue that the insurer cannot escape or reduce quantum by raising policy breach defences, which go to liability not quantum.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about liability/breach, not quantum reduction. If your appeal is purely on quantum (excessive award, wrong multiplier, wrong future prospects), this case is irrelevant.
adverse.quote: the quantum of compensation... cannot be said to be excessive or on the higher side

priority_arguments: 1. **Wrong multiplier applied**: Argue that the Tribunal applied a multiplier inconsistent with Sarla Verma (e.g., used the age of the eldest claimant instead of the deceased's age, or used a multiplier from the Second Schedule under Section 163A for a Section 166 claim). Cite doc_019 (Surendra Singh) which confirms the multiplier must be based on the deceased's age.

2. **Wrong future prospects**: Argue that the Tribunal added future prospects for a self-employed/temporary worker where Pranay Sethi does not permit it. Cite doc_033 (Satto) which held 'no addition towards future prospects' for a non-permanent worker.

3. **Non-dependent claimant**: Argue that a claimant who was not dependent on the deceased is not entitled to loss of dependency. Cite doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) where the court reduced compensation on this ground.

4. **Excessive interest rate**: Argue that the interest rate (often 9%) should be reduced to 6-7.5% given falling interest rates. Cite doc_004 (Soma Devi) reducing to 6% and doc_023 (Suman Lata) reducing to 7.5%.
5. **Contributory negligence**: If facts support it, argue for a deduction. Cite doc_009 (Kamal) for 50% deduction where the victim drove without licence/helmet.

6. **Computational errors**: Argue that the Tribunal made arithmetical errors (wrong deduction percentage, wrong dependency calculation). Cite doc_001 (Neelam Devi) where the court recalculated on the insurer's appeal.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without specific facts. Use compute_quantum tool with the actual income, age, and dependents data from your case.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The compensation range depends entirely on the facts of your case. Use the compute_quantum tool with the deceased's monthly income, age, number of dependents, and employment type to get the correct Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi calculation. Compare this with the Tribunal's award to identify the specific heads where the Tribunal erred.
risks: 1. **Enhancement risk (HIGH)**: The most significant risk is that the appellate court, under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC, may enhance the award if it finds the Tribunal's compensation was inadequate. This happened in doc_004 and doc_019. Mitigation: Before appealing, verify that the Tribunal's award is already at or above the Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi standards. If the Tribunal under-calculated, do NOT appeal quantum alone.

2. **Section 170 bar (HIGH)**: If the insurer did not obtain permission under Section 170 (because the insured contested the claim), the appeal on quantum may be dismissed in limine. Mitigation: Check the Tribunal record. If the insured/owner contested, the insurer's appeal may be limited to statutory defences under Section 149(2). Consider appealing only on legal/computational errors rather than factual quantum.

3. **Finding of fact (MEDIUM)**: Quantum assessments involve findings of fact (income assessment, dependency). Appellate courts are reluctant to interfere unless the finding is perverse or based on no evidence. Mitigation: Frame arguments as errors of law (wrong multiplier, wrong legal principle) rather than re-appreciation of evidence.

4. **Costs risk (LOW)**: Courts have deprecated insurers routinely appealing genuine claims. If the appeal is found to be frivolous, costs may be imposed. Mitigation: Only appeal if there is a clear legal error, not merely to delay payment.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: High Court under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The appeal should be confined to specific legal errors (wrong multiplier, wrong future prospects, wrong dependency calculation) rather than a general challenge to quantum. Consider also filing for reduction of interest rate as a fallback position.

args.question: Which judgments support reducing an award on appeal (quantum appeal by insurer), and which cut against me?

supporting.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
supporting.principle: A legal representative who was not dependent on the deceased is not entitled to compensation under 'loss of dependency'; only dependent legal representatives can claim under that head.
supporting.fact_alignment: Insurer appealed quantum on the ground that one claimant was gainfully employed and not dependent. The court agreed and reduced compensation by recalculating dependency and deduction.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent: the insurer's appeal on quantum succeeded, and the court actually reduced the award. It establishes that the insurer can successfully challenge the dependency calculation where a claimant is not genuinely dependent.
supporting.quote: a legal representative of a victim of a motor accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: Future prospects should not be added where the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer challenged addition of 50% towards future prospects for a deceased who was a fruit supplier (self-employed). The court held no addition for future prospects was warranted.
supporting.why_it_matters: Directly supports reducing quantum where the Tribunal wrongly added future prospects for a self-employed or temporary worker. This is a common error in Tribunal awards.
supporting.quote: Since the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment, he would not be entitled to any addition towards future prospects.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: The court can reduce the rate of interest on compensation on the insurer's appeal, even while upholding the principal quantum.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer appealed quantum; the court dismissed the appeal on quantum but reduced interest from 9% to 7.5% per annum.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that even where the principal quantum is upheld, the insurer can obtain meaningful relief by reducing the interest rate. Also establishes the important limitation that an insurer without Section 170 permission cannot challenge quantum.
supporting.quote: the interest should be reduced to 7.5% per annum

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: The court has power under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC to adjust compensation, including reducing interest rates, even when the insurer appeals.
supporting.fact_alignment: Insurer appealed quantum; court enhanced principal compensation but reduced interest from 7.5% to 6% per annum.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supports the proposition that interest rates can be reduced on appeal. Also confirms the court's wide power to modify awards under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC, which can work both ways.
supporting.quote: the prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum

supporting.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
supporting.principle: Contributory negligence (driving without licence and without helmet) justifies a 50% deduction from compensation.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Tribunal deducted 50% for contributory negligence where the injured rider had no licence and no helmet.
supporting.why_it_matters: If the facts of your case involve any contributory negligence by the victim (e.g., no helmet, no licence, driving on wrong side), this precedent supports a reduction in quantum on appeal.
supporting.quote: 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: The court can recalculate compensation on the insurer's appeal where the Tribunal applied wrong principles (e.g., wrong multiplier, wrong deduction, wrong future prospects).
supporting.fact_alignment: Insurer appealed quantum arguing income was assessed too high and future prospects wrongly applied. The court recalculated compensation using correct multiplier and deduction percentages in multiple connected cases.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that the insurer can successfully argue for recalculation where the Tribunal applied wrong multipliers or made computational errors. The court modified awards in multiple connected cases.
supporting.quote: the quantum of compensation awarded... stands modified

supporting.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
supporting.principle: Where the insurer is already impleaded as a party respondent, it can contest quantum on all grounds without being restricted to Section 149(2) defences.
supporting.fact_alignment: Insurer appealed quantum and contributory negligence finding; court dismissed appeal on facts but confirmed insurer's right to contest on all grounds when impleaded.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supports the insurer's procedural right to challenge quantum on appeal when impleaded as a party (even without Section 170 permission). The ratio on burden of proof for contributory negligence is useful for framing arguments.
supporting.quote: Once the insurer is impleaded... it would be entitled to contest the claim petition by raising all grounds without being restricted to the statutory defences under Section 149(2)

adverse.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
adverse.principle: An insurer without permission under Section 170 of the Motor Vehicles Act cannot challenge the quantum of compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will argue that your insurer client lacks standing to challenge quantum because it did not obtain Section 170 permission from the Tribunal. This is a jurisdictional bar that could get the appeal dismissed in limine.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This limitation applies only where the insurer was not impleaded as a party and the insured (owner) contested the claim. If the insurer was already impleaded as a party respondent (as in doc_018), or if the insured/owner failed to contest (collusion/absence), the insurer can challenge quantum on all grounds. Also, the insurer can always challenge on statutory defences under Section 149(2) and can argue computational/legal errors (wrong multiplier, wrong future prospects) as going to 'just compensation' rather than quantum per se.
adverse.quote: the Assurance Company cannot challenge the quantum of compensation without having permission under Section 170 of the Act

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC, the appellate court can enhance compensation even when only the insurer has appealed, because the court must award 'just compensation'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will argue that if the insurer appeals quantum, the court may use Order 41 Rule 33 CPC to enhance the award rather than reduce it. This is a real risk: the court in this very case enhanced compensation from ~Rs. 3.5 lakh to Rs. 5.99 lakh despite the insurer's appeal.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The enhancement risk is highest where the Tribunal's award is demonstrably below the Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi standards. If your Tribunal award already applies correct multipliers, future prospects, and deductions, the risk of enhancement is low. Also, the court reduced the interest rate in this case, showing it can adjust both ways.
adverse.quote: the court is duty-bound to award just compensation and may enhance the compensation amount under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC even in the absence of an appeal or cross-objections by the claimant

adverse.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
adverse.principle: The appellate court has a duty under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance inadequate compensation to ensure a 'just award', even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this for the proposition that an insurer's appeal opens the door to enhancement. The court here explicitly held that 'these proceedings being not truly adversarial' and that the court cannot 'close its eyes' to an inadequate award.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved clear errors in multiplier selection and failure to apply future prospects. If your Tribunal's award is already compliant with Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi standards, the risk of enhancement is minimal. The court's power under Order XLI Rule 33 is corrective, not punitive.
adverse.quote: the enhancement proposed is really in the nature of correction of the award on the basis of correct multiplier or principle or formula being applied in accordance with law laid down by the Supreme Court

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Where there is consistent oral testimony of an eye-witness, the Tribunal cannot impose contributory negligence based solely on a police sketch/site plan.
adverse.risk_to_client: If your appeal argues contributory negligence to reduce quantum, the opposing side will cite this to argue that the Tribunal's finding of no contributory negligence should not be disturbed unless the insurer led positive evidence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the specific fact that the insurer led NO evidence to rebut the eye-witness. If your case has independent evidence (e.g., site plan showing head-on collision, criminal court findings, or admissions in cross-examination), this precedent is distinguishable.
adverse.quote: once there is clinching oral evidence... that deceased was not negligent... the Tribunal cannot hold the deceased responsible for 50% negligence only on the basis of sketch/site plan

adverse.title: Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria vs Dilipkumar Ranchhodbhai Damor
adverse.principle: In injury cases, functional disability must be assessed in relation to the victim's vocation, and future prospects must be added even for self-employed persons.

supporting.why_it_matters: Directly supports reducing quantum where the Tribunal wrongly added future prospects for a self-employed or temporary worker. This is a common error in Tribunal awards.
supporting.quote: Since the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment, he would not be entitled to any addition towards future prospects.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
